gather.title: Why teams look for a Gather alternative
body: Gather made the virtual office popular, and for years a small team could use it for free. On September 15, 2025 that ended: Gather moved to $15 a member a month, or $12 billed yearly, and closed free offices that didn't upgrade. Teams that had locked in the old yearly price of $5.95 kept it until September 2026, so many of them are meeting the new price at this year's renewal.

Price isn't the only reason. Gather 2.0 is a new platform, and moving to it means building your office again. And many teams find they use a fraction of what they pay for: they want to see who's around, talk without scheduling, and meet. That's what the alternatives below are judged on.

items.title: TinyFloor
items.detail: $29 a month for the whole team, free for up to 3
items.body: A pixel-art office that opens in a browser tab, on a laptop or a phone. You see who's at their desk, walk up to talk, and step into the meeting room for video and screen sharing; there's team chat and a desk of your own. One price covers everyone you invite. It has no office editor, recordings, transcription or single sign-on, so teams that rely on those should look at Gather or Kumospace.

items.title: SoWork
items.detail: Basic $5.40 a member a month billed yearly; free for up to 10
items.body: The cheapest per-person plan here, and the most generous free plan for a team: up to 10 members, with meetings capped at 30 minutes. It's priced per member, so the bill grows with the team.

items.title: Kumospace
items.detail: Business from $16 a user a month; free for up to 5 members
items.body: A polished virtual office with desktop and mobile apps as well as the browser. Its free plan fits 5 members, 50 guests and one floor. For a team of 8 it's the most expensive option on this list after Gather's monthly plan.

items.title: WorkAdventure
items.detail: Business from $9 a user a month; free for up to 10 at once
items.body: Another pixel-art office, and open source, so a technical team can customise the map. Its free plan counts people online at the same time, up to 10, rather than members.

items.title: Teamflow
items.detail: $15 a person a month billed yearly; free for up to 5
items.body: A virtual office that runs as a desktop app for Mac and Windows, with mobile in beta. The free plan fits 5 people with 45-minute meetings. Billed yearly, it costs more per person than Gather's $12.

items.title: Roam
items.detail: A monthly price per active member; 14-day trial
items.body: A virtual office bundled with AI tools, in a desktop app you download. It charges only for members who are active, and has no free plan.

items.title: Discord
items.body: Not a virtual office, but many small teams already use its voice channels as one: drop in, talk, leave. It's free and the audio is good. It was built for gaming communities, so there's no office to see who's around, and work lives next to everything else on it.

items.title: Count the people who'll really use it
items.body: Free plans stop at 3 to 10 people, and most paid plans charge each person. For a team of 4 to 15, a flat price or a free plan that fits often beats a price per head.

items.title: Browser or app
items.body: Browser-only products need nothing installed and work for guests and contractors straight away. Desktop apps can do more, but everyone has to install them.

items.title: List your must-haves first
items.body: If you need recordings, transcripts, an office you design yourself or single sign-on, that narrows the list to Gather, Kumospace and a few others, whatever the price.

items.title: Try it on a normal working day
items.body: These tools prove themselves in the small moments: a quick question, a meeting that starts on time. A week of real work tells you more than a demo.

virtualOffice.title: What a virtual office is, and isn't
body: "Virtual office" means two different things. One is a business address: a service that gives a company a mailing address and sometimes a phone line, without a desk. The other, and the one this page is about, is an online office where a remote team works together during the day.

That second kind is a shared space that stays open while people work. Instead of a grid of faces that ends when a meeting does, everyone has a place in the office, can see who else is around, and starts a conversation the way you would in a building: by going over to someone.

items.title: See who's in
items.body: Everyone appears in the office, with a status, so you know who's at their desk, who's busy and who's in a meeting before you interrupt.

items.title: Talk without scheduling
items.body: Walk up to a teammate and start talking. A two-minute question stays two minutes, instead of becoming a calendar invite for tomorrow.

items.title: Meet in a room
items.body: Group conversations happen in a meeting room you walk into, with video and screen sharing, and you walk out when it's done.

items.title: Have a desk of your own
items.body: A desk gives each person a place, so the office looks like a team rather than a lobby.

items.title: Chat beside it
items.body: Messages and channels sit next to the floor, for what doesn't need talking.

discord.title: Why teams use Discord as an office
body: Plenty of small teams, especially developers, studios and startups, run their day in Discord. They make a server, open a voice channel, and people drop in and out the way they would walk into a shared room. It's free, the audio is good, screen sharing works in voice channels, and there's nothing new to learn for anyone who already uses it.
What it shows is that being one click from each other works better than scheduling every conversation. The question is whether an app built for gaming communities is the best home for that.

discord.title: Where it falls short for work

items.title: It's personal, not your company's
items.body: People join with their own Discord accounts, so work sits next to their gaming servers and friends, with every notification in one place.

items.title: Channels instead of a place
items.body: You see who's in which voice channel, but not who's at their desk and free for a minute. Joining a channel is an all-or-nothing way to start talking.

items.title: No obvious meeting room
items.body: A meeting is another voice channel. It works, but there's no sense of stepping into a room and back out to your desk.

items.title: Built around communities
items.body: Roles, servers and bots are made for large groups of strangers. A team of eight needs much less, and more of what an office has.

standup.title: How a standup runs on TinyFloor
body: Every office has a main meeting that's always open. Standup is that room at the same time every day: nobody sends a link, and nobody waits in a lobby for a host.

items.title: Walk in
items.body: Join the main meeting and your character walks into the meeting room. Everyone on the floor can see the room filling up.

items.title: Go round
items.body: Voice first, cameras if people want them. Whoever is talking takes the big card, so it's clear who has the floor.

items.title: Walk out
items.body: Walk out of the room to leave, and go back to your desk. Anything that needs more than a minute carries on at someone's desk with the two people it concerns.

standup.title: Three formats that work
body: Pick one and keep it. A standup that changes shape every week turns into a status meeting.

head: Format
How it goes
Suits
rows: Each person: what I finished, what I'm on today, what's in my way.
New teams, and teams whose work doesn't sit on one board.
Go through the board from right to left, the work closest to done first. People speak when their card comes up.
Teams that share a Kanban or sprint board. Share it on screen.
One line and a parking lot
One sentence each, then the questions that came up, taken by whoever needs them.
Small, settled teams that talk all day anyway.

standup.title: How long it should take
body: Plan on about a minute a person and a couple of minutes for the parking lot. Past 12 or so, a round takes longer than people can listen; split by project, or walk the board instead.

head: Team
Round
With the parking lot
rows: split it, or walk the board
table.note: A rule of thumb, not a timer. A 15-minute standup every working day comes to about 5 hours of meetings a month, on any plan.

items.title: Start on time
items.body: Start at the minute even if someone's missing. The floor shows who's in, who's away and who's still on a call, so you can tell who to wait for and who not to.

items.title: Take follow-ups to a desk
items.body: When two people need to dig into something, they walk to a desk after standup. The rest of the room doesn't have to listen.

items.title: Show, don't describe
items.body: Share a window for the board or a bug instead of reading it out. One click, and it's on everyone's screen.

items.title: Leave cameras optional
items.body: Anyone without a camera shows as a card that lights up when they talk. A camera that's been on through ten quiet minutes turns itself off.

standup.title: Live, written, or both
body: A team spread across time zones can't always meet at one time. Many post a written update in a channel of the office's chat, and keep the live standup for the days with something to decide: a release, a problem, a new person.

items.title: Live
items.body: Quicker to unblock, and it's the one time a day the whole team is in one room. Best when most of you share working hours.

items.title: Written
items.body: Works across time zones and leaves a record. Easy to skim, easy to skip, so blockers can sit unnoticed.

items.title: Both
items.body: Written updates every day, and a short live round once or twice a week, at a time that suits everyone.

standup.title: What TinyFloor doesn't do for standups
body: There's no standup bot that asks the questions for you, no reminder, no timer and no recording. It doesn't connect to Jira, Linear or GitHub, so the board goes on screen as a shared window. If you need written standups collected automatically, a bot in your chat tool does that better; TinyFloor is where the team meets.

pairProgramming.title: How a pairing session starts
body: In an office, pairing often starts with "got a minute?" at someone's desk. Remote, it usually needs a calendar invite, so it happens less. On TinyFloor it starts the way it did in the office.

items.title: See who's free
items.body: Desks and statuses show who's heads down, who's away and who's already in a call. Busy means wait; available means walk over.

items.title: Walk over and talk
items.body: Stand next to them and tap to call. It starts with voice; turn a camera on if you want one.

items.title: Share and work
items.body: Share a window, a tab or your whole screen: the editor, the terminal, the failing test.

items.title: Walk back
items.body: Hang up and you're back at your own work. The call stays connected while you move, so nothing drops if you wander.

pairProgramming.title: Pairing styles that work remotely
body: Every style below works with one person sharing and both talking. To swap who drives, push a work-in-progress branch and the other person shares their screen instead.

head: Style
How it goes
Good for
rows: One types, the other thinks ahead, reads and catches mistakes. Swap every 20 to 30 minutes.
Most pairing, and bringing someone into unfamiliar code.
One writes a failing test, the other makes it pass and writes the next test.
Test-driven work, and keeping both people equally involved.
Ideas go into the code only through the other person's hands: the navigator says what, the driver types it.
Teaching and onboarding, so the newer person isn't just watching.
Ten minutes on someone else's problem, then walk back.
The quick question that would otherwise wait for tomorrow.

pairProgramming.title: Making shared code easy to read

items.title: Share one window
items.body: A shared screen is tuned for sharp text rather than smooth motion. A single editor window reads better than a whole wide monitor scaled down.

items.title: Turn the font up
items.body: Go up two or three sizes in the editor and terminal while you pair. What's comfortable on your screen is small on theirs.

items.title: Keep it in one place
items.body: Split the editor and terminal in the same window, so the share doesn't need switching every time a test runs.

items.title: Say where you're looking
items.body: Point by file and line number: "line 84 in the handler" beats "up a bit, no, there".

pairProgramming.title: When two becomes three
body: Walk up to a third teammate during a call and TinyFloor offers to make it a meeting for the three of you. For a planned mob or ensemble session, use the meeting room: whoever is talking takes the big card, and the shared screen sits beside the people.

pairProgramming.title: What to use alongside it
body: TinyFloor is where you find each other and talk. It doesn't do everything a pairing session can need:

items.title: No remote control
items.body: The other person can see your screen but can't type into it. For both people editing the same code, use your editor's own tool, such as VS Code Live Share or JetBrains Code With Me, and keep TinyFloor for the voice.

items.title: No sound from the shared screen
items.body: Screen sharing carries the picture only, which is what code needs.

items.title: No recording
items.body: Sessions aren't recorded. Write down what you decided in the pull request or the team chat.

items.title: No GitHub or Jira connection
items.body: Share the pull request or the ticket on screen to look at it together.

items.title: Respect busy
items.body: A busy status is the closed door. Send a message in the chat instead, and let them come to you.

items.title: Keep sessions short
items.body: An hour or two at most, with breaks. Pairing all day is tiring, even when it's going well.

items.title: Make asking normal
items.body: A team where people walk over with questions unblocks in minutes, not tomorrow. Seniors walking over to juniors helps as much as the other way round.

onboarding.title: A new person's first day on the floor
body: On a remote team, nobody can see that someone new has started. On the floor they can: there's a new name at a desk, and the team is a short walk away.

items.title: Open the invite link
items.body: One link for the whole office. Sign in with Google or an email address, in the browser, with nothing to install.

items.title: Pick a desk
items.body: You arrive beside a free desk. Sit down and make it yours; from then on nobody else sits there.

items.title: Get a wave
items.body: Everyone already on the floor sees you walk in and can wave. It's a small thing, and it tells the new person they've been noticed.

items.title: Say hello at standup
items.body: Walk into the meeting room with everyone else. One minute to introduce yourself, and the team has met you.

items.title: Sit with your buddy
items.body: Walk over to your buddy's desk, share a screen and work through the first task together.

onboarding.title: A first week that works

Standup intro, then most of the day at the buddy's desk.
Finish the first task. Short calls with two or three people from other parts of the work.
Walk over to each of them for fifteen minutes.
A second task, more on their own. Questions as they come.

Sit in on a review, a planning session or a client call.
Join a meeting in the meeting room; listening counts.

items.title: Knowing who to ask
items.body: In an office you learn who knows what by watching who people go to. On the floor, you can see the same thing: who's talking to whom, and who's busy.

items.title: Asking without feeling like an interruption
items.body: Sending a message to someone you've never met feels like a lot. Walking up to an available person is the same as leaning over in an office.

items.title: Being seen working
items.body: A new person at a desk is visibly part of the team from day one, instead of a name in a channel.

items.title: Overhearing how the team works
items.body: Sitting in on a meeting or two teaches more about how decisions get made than any document.

onboarding.title: Making the buddy system work remotely

items.title: Pick someone close to the work
items.body: Not the manager, and not the busiest person on the team. Someone who does similar work and has time for questions.

items.title: Book time on the first two days
items.body: Most of Monday and some of Tuesday together, sharing a screen. After that, the new person walks over when they need to.

items.title: Make the first visit for them
items.body: The buddy walks over first, on day one. It shows the new person that walking over is normal here.

items.title: Keep a channel for questions
items.body: A channel in the team chat for questions nobody should feel silly asking. Messages stay, so the next new person can read the answers.

onboarding.title: What TinyFloor doesn't do for onboarding
body: It isn't an HR tool. There are no onboarding checklists, document signing, account provisioning or single sign-on. Keep your handbook in your docs tool and your accounts in your admin tools; TinyFloor is where the new person meets the team and gets help. Inviting them takes one link, and they can be at a desk a minute later.

watercooler.title: What the watercooler was really for
body: Nobody misses the water. What remote teams miss is the conversation nobody planned: the question asked on the way past, the joke, the five minutes that made someone feel part of the team. In Gallup's 2024 data, 25% of fully remote workers reported loneliness, against 16% of people on site.
Scheduled social calls try to fix that and often feel like another meeting. What works better is giving people a place where running into each other can happen again.

watercooler.title: How it happens on the floor

items.title: Someone walks in
items.body: When a teammate arrives, everyone already on the floor sees a quiet "Ana is in" with a wave button for a few seconds. One wave, and the day has started with a hello.

items.title: You pass someone
items.body: Walking to the meeting room or the whiteboard, you go past desks. Stop next to someone and a call is one tap away; walk on and nothing happens.

items.title: Music in the room
items.body: Walk up to the speaker and put a track on. Everyone hears the same song, loud near the speaker and fading as they walk away, so people at their desks can still work.

items.title: The chat between calls
items.body: A channel for anything that isn't work, with emoji and reactions. Messages stay, so nobody misses the joke because they were in a meeting.

watercooler.title: Rituals that work for a small team
body: Keep them short, optional and regular. A team of eight doesn't need an events programme; it needs a few habits people actually turn up for.

head: Ritual
How it goes
How often
rows: Start a meeting called Coffee and ask everyone in. Fifteen minutes, no agenda, cameras optional.
Someone shares their screen for five minutes: a side project, a photo, a tool they like.
A message in a channel on Friday afternoon, one line each.
Leave something on the shared whiteboard for the morning: a question, a drawing, a poll.
People who feel like it eat at their desks with the office open and chat if they want to.

items.title: Making it mandatory
items.body: A social call people have to attend is a meeting. Invite, and don't count who came.

items.title: Cameras required
items.body: Being watched is tiring. Voice-first conversations are easier to drop into, and anyone without a camera still shows as a card that lights up when they talk.

items.title: Points and leaderboards
items.body: Streaks and badges turn time together into a contest. TinyFloor doesn't have them, on purpose.

items.title: Watching who's online
items.body: Nothing on the floor counts how long anyone has been there or how long they've been idle. People relax when nobody's keeping score.

watercooler.title: What TinyFloor doesn't do
body: There are no games, no trivia, no YouTube screens and no event spaces for a hundred guests. It's a small office for a team that works together every day, and the watercooler is the part between tasks. For a company party or a large social event, Kumospace and Gather have more built in.

engineering.title: An engineering day on the floor
body: Engineers need two things that pull against each other: long stretches without interruptions, and a quick answer when they're stuck. A floor gives you both, because you can see who's heads down before you walk over.

items.title: Standup
items.body: The team walks into the meeting room, goes round in ten minutes and walks back out.

items.title: Heads down
items.body: Set yourself busy. You're still on the floor, so people know you're working, and they know to wait.

items.title: Unblocked
items.body: Stuck on a failing build? See who's available, walk over, share the logs and sort it out in ten minutes instead of tomorrow.

items.title: Review
items.body: Two or three people in a meeting, one sharing the pull request, talking it through instead of forty comments.

engineering.title: How it fits beside your tools
body: TinyFloor runs in a browser tab next to your editor, terminal and chat. It doesn't connect to GitHub, GitLab, Jira or Linear, and it doesn't post into Slack. meetingRoom.title: How a meeting works on TinyFloor

items.title: Talk

items.title: Share
items.body: Share a window, a tab or your screen. It goes on the stage next to the people.

items.title: Walk out
items.body: Leave and you're back on the floor. Walked out by mistake? Rejoin is one press.

presence.title: Using presence well as a team

body: Presence doesn't sync with your calendar, Slack or your operating system, and statuses don't change on a schedule. There are no custom status messages yet. body: It's a pen-and-eraser board. There's no text tool, no shapes or sticky notes, no images, no undo, no templates and no export, and an office has one board rather than many. For workshops, retrospectives with sticky notes or detailed diagrams, Miro, FigJam or Excalidraw do far more. The TinyFloor board is for the quick sketch while you talk.

agencies.title: A day at a small agency on the floor

virtualCoworking.title: Why working near others helps
body: Studies of ambient awareness at work found that seeing colleagues' presence at a glance made people feel others were working too, and led to more informal contact. In Gallup's 2024 data, fully remote workers reported loneliness more often than people on site, 25% against 16%. A floor where your team is visibly around addresses both, without anyone having to be on camera.

virtualCoworking.title: What it isn't
body: TinyFloor isn't a public coworking space. An office is private to your team, so there are no strangers to work alongside and no matching with other people. There are no session timers, no streaks and nothing that counts how long you worked. If you work alone and want company from strangers, a body-doubling service is the better fit; if you want your team around while you work, this is it.

features.title: How the pieces fit
body: A TinyFloor office is one shared floor: a desk for everyone, a meeting room that's always open, a whiteboard on the wall and a chat beside it all. You move around as a character, and where you stand decides who you talk to.
Every plan has every feature, the free one included. What changes with Pro is how many people the office holds, not what they can do.

features.title: What's left out on purpose
body: There's no recording, no tracking of how long anyone is online and no integrations to set up. Microphones are off until a call starts, and cameras rest when nobody's talking. It runs in the browser on desktop and mobile, with nothing to install.

teams.title: One floor, different days
body: Small remote teams tend to share the same two problems: a quick question takes too long to ask, and nobody can see who's around. What differs is the rhythm of the day.

Engineers need long stretches of focus and a fast way to get unstuck. Designers need feedback many times a day. Agencies juggle clients and freelancers. Startups need speed, and a price that doesn't grow with every hire. Hybrid teams need the people at home to be as present as the people in the office.

body: Each page walks through a typical day for that kind of team, what to keep in your other tools, and where TinyFloor isn't the right fit.

useCases.title: The workday, moment by moment
body: A remote workday is mostly quiet work, broken up by a handful of moments when people need each other: the morning standup, a question to a colleague, a new person's first week, a few minutes of chat between tasks.
Each page takes one of those moments and shows how it runs on the floor, with the formats, timings and habits small teams use, and what TinyFloor doesn't do, so you can pick the right tool for each.

hybrid.title: Why hybrid is hard on the people at home
body: In a hybrid team, the decisions still happen where most people are. A question asked across a desk, a chat by the coffee machine, a meeting that starts early because everyone's already in the room: the people at home only hear about it later, if at all.
Video calls don't fix that, because the conversations that matter weren't meetings. The fix is a place where everyone is equally present, whichever building they're in.

items.title: Everyone joins from their own laptop
items.body: In the office or at home, each person opens the same floor, so nobody is a face on a screen in someone else's room.

items.title: See who's around, wherever they are
items.body: Available, busy, away, in a call, in the meeting room: the same signals for everyone, so you know who you can ask.

items.title: Walk over instead of messaging
items.body: A question to a colleague at home is the same short walk as one to the person at the next desk.

items.title: Meetings in one room
items.body: Hold the standup in the meeting room with everyone on their own laptop, instead of a room full of people and a few faces on a screen.

items.title: If one is remote, everyone is remote
items.body: When anyone in a meeting is at home, everyone joins from their own laptop, even people sitting in the same room.

items.title: Decisions get written down
items.body: Anything decided in the building goes in the team chat, so the people at home see it the same day.

items.title: Headphones in the office
items.body: People in the building use headphones on the floor, so their calls don't echo and their neighbours aren't disturbed.

items.title: Office days aren't meeting days
items.body: Don't save every meeting for the days people are in. If the meeting room works for everyone, use it every day.
